rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra’s common theme is truth and falsehood in conflict: the Prophet and believers ultimately succeed, while Quraysh are defeated and warned.
rows.anchor: the conflict between truth and falsehood which has ensued because of the Prophet’s preaching

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs in human life and the universe, considered through sense and reason, show Quraysh the evil outcome of continuing to oppose revealed truth.
rows.anchor: Through the testimony of sense and reason and through the signs found in a person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and companions should remain steadfast and pious; divine practice brings truth to victory through trials, leading to success in both worlds.
rows.anchor: it is God’s established practice that the truth triumphs after necessarily passing through various trials and tribulations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike earlier sūras’ accounts of many messengers, this sūra tells one comprehensive account, called the best anecdote.
rows.anchor: just one anecdote is comprehensively taken up. It has been called “the best anecdote.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending summarizes that God does not waste the reward of those who fear Him and remain steadfast; the episode corroborates the historical testimony in Hūd.
rows.anchor: those who fear God and remain steadfast, then God does not waste the reward

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s story mirrors the Prophet’s future ordeals and victories, including plots against his life, escape, migration to Madinah, and the believers’ rise to power.
rows.anchor: the account of Joseph (sws) in particular mirrors the situations that the Prophet (sws) will face from his adversaries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s pardon of his brothers parallels the Prophet’s pardon at the conquest of Makkah, when former enemies acknowledged his goodness.
rows.anchor: I will say the same thing to you what Joseph (sws) said to his brothers: “Go you are free. Today there is no blame on you.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story lets the Prophet see his own situation and lets discerning opponents see their fate; indirect narrative advice can affect readers more deeply than explicit admonition.
rows.anchor: Subtle accounts have a much more profound effect than explicit pieces of advice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account combines beauty and love with moral purity, nourishing faith and delighting the soul while presenting conduct people can realistically emulate.
rows.anchor: it has the sweetness of beauty and love in it. Yet Joseph (sws) who is the central character

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although its events are astonishing, their sequence feels natural and harmonious, so readers readily accept and are moved by the story’s truth.
rows.anchor: at no place does it seem that anything in them is out of order and sequence

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s trials reveal intelligence, truthfulness, purity, chastity, and forgiveness despite having power to take revenge; these are not the story’s only lessons.
rows.anchor: He comes out as an abiding example of intelligence, truthfulness, purity, chastity and a person who is an embodiment of forgiveness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reconstructs a suppressed phrase meaning “in order to choose him”; the coordinating wāw signals its omission, and the translation supplies the complete sentence.
rows.anchor: the particle of co-ordination وand) points to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Egyptian buyer was a senior royal-guard official and decent man; the Torah indicates he recognized Joseph as noble-born rather than a slave when he saw him.
rows.anchor: It is evident from the Torah that as soon as he saw Joseph (sws), he understood that he was not a slave

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The buyer may have been childless and hoped to adopt Joseph if he met expectations; the Bible indicates he placed Joseph in charge of his household.
rows.anchor: until that time he was issueless and thus thought that if the boy fulfilled his expectations, he would adopt him as a son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God carries out His will summarizes the story so far and warns Quraysh that they can see their own future in Joseph’s story and the Prophet’s plots.
rows.anchor: sum the anecdote of Joseph (sws) thus far narrated. It may be kept in mind that it is being narrated to the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ashudd can mean youth or mature age; the mature-age sense also occurs in al-Aḥqāf.
rows.anchor: is used both for youth as well as for mature age. The latter usage can be see in verse 15 of Sūrah al-Aḥqāf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired gifts of judgment and knowledge signify prophethood: judgment includes decision-making and political authority, while knowledge is revelation given to prophets.
rows.anchor: here signify prophethood. The first of them means the power of decision-making as well as political authority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph received these gifts because he recognized his obligations to God and passed every test, so God appointed him a prophet.
rows.anchor: he understood his rights and obligations to God and passed every test. As a result, God appointed him a prophet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Joseph passed the brothers’ jealousy and enmity, a second, tougher test began when the Egyptian official’s wife tried to seduce him; it led to unjust imprisonment.
rows.anchor: enticing him with her love.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As in the first trial, God granted Joseph great success in this second phase.
rows.anchor: just a he passed the first test, he was given grand success by God in this second phase too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression “warāwadat-hu ʿan nafsihi” means she tried to deceive Joseph into adultery.
rows.anchor: means that she tried to deceive him into adultery.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “hayta laka” means “come forth.”
rows.anchor: The words !ۡ!!!ﻫﻴﺖ ﻟﻚ mean ﻫﻠﻢ ﻟﻚ وcome forth)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here rabb has its ordinary literal sense of master or owner, as it does in verses 41 and 42.
rows.anchor: here is used in its general literal meaning of master and owner.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The temptation of love and lust followed the brothers’ hatred and jealousy, and was a harder trial for Joseph.
rows.anchor: this trial was far tougher than the previous one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s reply is psychologically eloquent: he reminds her that a small kindness from his master won his deep loyalty, while she betrays her husband despite being his wife and mistress of his household.
rows.anchor: emotions was like casting pearls before a swine.

rows.speaker: some exegetes
rows.claim: Some exegetes take the pronoun in “innahu rabbi” to refer to God.
rows.anchor: Some exegetes opine that the antecedent of the accusative pronoun in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The context does not support taking the pronoun as referring to God; the author finds that reading an overextension.
rows.anchor: However, this is over-stretching the mind. The context does not support it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear sign is an innate divine spark that distinguishes right from wrong and urges good while restraining evil.
rows.anchor: here refers to the divine spark

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God strengthens this spark in those who heed its guidance until it protects them from temptation; neglect makes it fade or die, leaving people morally insensitive.
rows.anchor: it becomes ever stronger in those who duly value it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph valued this inner guidance and it guarded him; Islahi estimates that he was about eighteen to twenty and might otherwise have succumbed.
rows.anchor: He must be around 18-20 years.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic words can refer to both God and people, but their sense changes according to context.
rows.anchor: There are many words in a language that are used both for God and for people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s inner guidance flared at the temptation and immediately dispelled the darkness before him.
rows.anchor: It was on this occasion that it dazzled in his inner being

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Burhān means a clear proof or conclusive argument, and no proof is clearer than the one resounding from within a person.
rows.anchor: The word #ۡ!ﺑﺮﻫﺎن is used for clear proof and conclusive argument. What proof can be more clear and conclusive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets are protected from sin before appointment, but infallibility does not mean they lack the capacity to sin; they preserve an inner spark that withstands great trials.
rows.anchor: God protects them from sins even before they are appointed as prophets. Second, this infallibility does not mean that a prophet does not have the potential to commit sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istibāq means trying to outdo one another in a race.
rows.anchor: means to try and outdo one another in a race.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wife tried to clear herself before her husband and make Joseph appear guilty; the torn shirt served as circumstantial evidence for resolving the dispute.
rows.anchor: if any circumstantial evidence could be helpful in resolving the dispute, it was the torn shirt of Joseph (sws).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural “your plot” intensifies the husband’s anger, as if the wife’s act made all women seem deceptive and loathsome to him.
rows.anchor: expresses the intensity of a man’s anger.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repentance was important in polytheistic religions too.
rows.anchor: repentance held great importance in polytheistic religions as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAzīz means a dominant, powerful person and can denote a king or high official; here it refers to a senior royal bodyguard.
rows.anchor: means someone who is dominant and powerful.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The city women’s words rebuke and challenge the wife: she stooped to pursue her husband’s slave but failed, while they boast they would have succeeded.
rows.anchor: The last sentence uttered by these women have many elements of rebuke, callousness and challenge in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hurt by their mockery, the wife gathered the women with fruit and knives, then summoned Joseph; his radiant beauty and noble conduct astonished them.
rows.anchor: When they came, she handed them knives to cut the fruit. After that she called Joseph (sws) to their presence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women first tried sweet talk, then threatened suicide and cut their hands as a plot to frighten Joseph into yielding; the Qur’an condenses this exchange, later confirmed at 12:50–51.
rows.anchor: they tried to lure him through their sweet talk. But when they saw their words were having no impact on Joseph

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anecdote from the author’s time in Bombay illustrates a beggar threatening self-immolation to pressure a shopkeeper, then stopping when the threat failed.
rows.anchor: Once I was sitting at the shop of a friend in Bombay when a beggar came and sat on the road.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Ḥāsha lillāh” excludes someone from bad traits; in “mā hādhā basharan,” mā means laysa, making bashar accusative.
rows.anchor: The expression !! %ٰ ﺣﺎش ﷲ is meant to show exception and absolve someone from bad traits.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The women’s confession praises Joseph’s nobility while excusing their failure as a consequence of facing someone angelic, rather than any defect in their beauty or scheme.
rows.anchor: This confession of the ladies is actually high praise for Joseph (sws) and also an excuse for their failure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zelicha felt relief at the other women’s humiliation, but then turned the failed lustful pursuit toward revenge; as a powerful official’s wife, she could send her slave to prison.
rows.anchor: Failure of love in its lust induces it to revenge. It seems that in those times masters had unlimited powers over their slaves.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zelicha threatened prison to pressure Joseph, but he preferred confinement to committing the evil she demanded.
rows.anchor: he preferred to go to prison than do such an evil thing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph prayed after exhausting his own strength in guarding his faith and choosing prison over elite women’s seduction.
rows.anchor: The prayer uttered by Joseph (sws) was at a time when he had spent his full strength

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When God’s servant perseveres, entrusts himself to God, and asks for help, his prayer is accepted immediately; Joseph escaped the women’s lustful trap.
rows.anchor: When a servant of God consigns himself to Him and seeks His help after showing so much perseverance then his prayer is definitely accepted

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God hears His servants’ requests and prayers and knows what is in their hearts.
rows.anchor: God hears the requests and prayers of His servants and is also fully aware of what is in their hearts.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joseph’s imprisonment begins another trial: his powerful hosts knew the reality but judged a short prison term would silence gossip and lessen Zelicha’s infatuation by keeping him away.
rows.anchor: they deemed it appropriate to send him to jail for some time. They must have thought that in this way people would stop gossiping about the whole issue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two inmates’ dreams and Joseph’s correct interpretations ultimately create the opportunity for him to interpret the reigning king’s dream, after which the king entrusts him with control of the kingdom.
rows.anchor: He does so and the interpretation proves to be absolutely true. Ultimately, this paves the way of he interpreting the dream seen by the reigning king.
